warmup.q: The refund from the opening changes two balances, on two different pages of a PostgreSQL table, as one transaction: a group of changes that must all happen or none. Then PostgreSQL answers COMMIT, its word for "done and saved". What has reached the disk at that moment?
options: Both table pages, written and forced to disk by COMMIT
Nothing yet: everything stays in memory until the database next saves all its pages
Small log records describing both changes and the commit, forced to disk, but neither table page
The two table pages, but not the log, which is written in the background
warmup.why: COMMIT forces the write-ahead log, the file of change records, up to the commit record, and returns. The table pages stay changed in memory only. They reach the disk later, written by a background process or a checkpoint; the first Try it shows both pages still waiting after COMMIT. If nothing had reached the disk, a crash would lose a refund the screen had called done. The last option has it backwards: the log must be safe on disk first.

sections.h: What a commit really writes: the log now, the pages later
sections.html:
Let's set up the refund in the Try it. PostgreSQL, a free database program, keeps a table of accounts with a balance in each row. A table is a file of 8 KB pages, and the two rows of our refund live on two of them: page 0 and page 132. The refund changes both. The two changes form one transaction, a group of changes that must all happen or none, and the moment the database promises they're saved is the commit. Both changes must survive a crash, and they must survive together.

Version 1 writes both pages to the table's file at commit and forces them to disk. Forcing means fsync, the request that makes the operating system push data all the way onto the drive instead of holding it in memory. Bytes, pages and durability: a log-structured store measured one at about 4 ms on a laptop. So that's two 8 KB writes at two places in the file, plus a force. And it isn't even safe. If the power fails after the first page is written and before the second, the shop's balance is down 25.00, the customer's isn't up, and nothing says the refund was half done.

Version 2 first copies the old contents of both pages to a separate journal file, then overwrites the pages. After a crash, a leftover journal means "put these pages back". That's the rollback journal, the default in SQLite, a small database built into many phone apps. It's all-or-nothing, but it still writes every changed page at commit, twice.

Version 3 is the write-ahead log (WAL). For every change, append a small record that describes it to one log file, the append-only kind from Bytes, pages and durability: "on page 132, set the balance in row 14 to 102,500". Change the pages only in memory, in the buffer pool, the database's own cache of pages from The buffer pool. At commit, append a commit record and force the log. That's one write at the end of one file, and one fsync, for the whole transaction. Transactions that commit at the same moment share that fsync, which is called group commit. In the second Try it, a refund like ours writes 200 bytes of log. Writing its two pages would be 16 KB.

The changed pages stay in memory, marked dirty, meaning they differ from the copy on disk. They reach the table's file later, in the background. If the power fails first, the log holds everything needed to redo them. PostgreSQL may even write a dirty page to disk before its transaction commits, when it needs the room in memory. The lab is simpler: a transaction's changes reach the pages only when it commits.

A café's back room works the same way. The stock counts sit on a whiteboard, quick to rub out and rewrite. But before anyone changes a number, they write the change in a notebook by the door: "took 2 bags of beans, 14 left". If the whiteboard gets wiped, the notebook can rebuild it. The notebook is the log, the whiteboard is the pages, and writing in the notebook first is the rule this lesson is named for.

The figure is the picture for this lesson. The log runs ahead and is forced at every commit. The table's files lag behind, and they're allowed to, because the log can rebuild them. Next, we'll make "the log can rebuild them" precise.

try.title: Commit leaves the pages dirty
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's window for SQL commands, with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.

Create accounts with 20,000 rows and find which pages hold rows 42 and 17042 (ctid is a row's address: page, then slot). Then run CHECKPOINT, which writes every changed page to disk, so that no page is dirty.

Run the refund between the two rows, from BEGIN to COMMIT. Predict which pages are dirty after COMMIT. Then compare page 0's LSN, a stamp from the log that the next section explains, in memory and in the first 8 bytes of the file on disk. Run CHECKPOINT and read the file again.

code.title: psql
code.html: CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, balance_cents bigint) WITH (fillfactor = 70, autovacuum_enabled = off); INSERT INTO accounts SELECT g, 100000 FROM generate_series(1, 20000) g; SELECT ctid FROM accounts WHERE id IN (42, 17042); CHECKPOINT; SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE isdirty) AS dirty_pages FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('accounts'); BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 2500 WHERE id = 42; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 2500 WHERE id = 17042; COMMIT; SELECT relblocknumber, isdirty FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('accounts') AND isdirty ORDER BY 1; SELECT lsn AS in_memory FROM page_header(get_raw_page('accounts', 0)); SELECT pg_relation_filepath('accounts') AS f \gset \setenv F :f \! od -A n -t x4 -N 8 /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker/$F CHECKPOINT; \! od -A n -t x4 -N 8 /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker/$F

After the COMMIT, the file still has the old LSN, 0/220F0A0, while the page in memory is at 0/24B8130: the commit wrote the log, not the page. The CHECKPOINT writes the page, and the file catches up. Your LSNs will differ. fillfactor = 70 leaves room on each page, so an update can put the new row version on the same page. Turning autovacuum off for this table keeps PostgreSQL's background clean-up, which the Transactions track's lesson on MVCC covers, out of the next Try it's log.

sections.h: Two rules keep the log ahead of the pages
sections.html:
The log can only rebuild a page if we can tell how far that page has got. So the database numbers its log. The LSN, the log sequence number, is a record's position in the log, counted in bytes from the start. PostgreSQL prints it as two numbers in hexadecimal (base 16), like 0/2F12D5D8. Two positions matter. One is where the next record will go (pg_current_wal_insert_lsn()). The other is how far the log is safe on disk, the flush LSN (pg_current_wal_flush_lsn()).

Each page carries one more, the page LSN, in the first 8 bytes of the page header from Pages, tuples and heap files. It's the position just past the last log record that changed the page. On the whiteboard, it's the notebook line number written next to each count.

Two rules use these numbers. The commit rule: COMMIT returns only after the flush LSN has passed the commit record. That's what makes a commit durable, safe through a crash.

The WAL rule, which gives the log its name: before a dirty page is written to the table's file, the log must be on disk at least up to that page's LSN. The log goes ahead of the data. Break the rule, and a crash can leave a page on disk holding a change that the log on disk never recorded. Recovery can't redo what it can't see, and it can't undo what it doesn't know about. In the lab, a refund's first page could reach the disk while its commit record is still in memory; one of the lab's tests stages exactly that crash.

In PostgreSQL, the code that manages the buffer pool enforces the rule. Before it writes a dirty page, it calls XLogFlush with the page's LSN, which flushes the log first if it has to. It rarely has to, because commits keep the log far ahead of the pages.

One setting relaxes the commit rule and keeps the WAL rule: synchronous_commit = off. COMMIT then returns without waiting for the flush. The WAL writer, a background process, flushes within at most three times wal_writer_delay, 600 ms by default. A crash can lose those last transactions entirely, but never half of one, because no page holding their changes can reach the disk ahead of their log records. The docs describe the risk as "some recent allegedly-committed transactions being lost". For a refund the screen has called done, leave it on.

Don't confuse it with fsync = off, which stops forcing anything at all. The WAL rule then no longer holds on disk, and the docs warn that a power cut can corrupt the database for good. Test setups turn it off for speed, and that setting has a way of following them into real use.

The Try it reads one refund's records with pg_waldump and finds each page's LSN equal to the end of the record that last changed it. Next, we'll crash the database and watch the log do its work.

try.title: Match page LSNs to log records
steps: VACUUM the table, which clears out the old row versions the first refund left behind. Then run a second refund, noting the log position before and after.
Dump exactly those bytes of log with pg_waldump, a tool that prints log records (it runs inside the container through \!). Predict how many records a two-row refund writes.
Read the page LSN of both pages and the flush LSN. Predict how each page LSN relates to the records.

code.title: psql
code.html: VACUUM accounts; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn() AS before \gset BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 1000 WHERE id = 42; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 1000 WHERE id = 17042; COMMIT; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn() AS after \gset SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff(:'after', :'before') AS wal_bytes; \setenv B :before \setenv E :after \! pg_waldump -p /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker/pg_wal -s $B -e $E SELECT 0 AS blk, lsn FROM page_header(get_raw_page('accounts', 0)) UNION ALL SELECT 132, lsn FROM page_header(get_raw_page('accounts', 132)); SELECT pg_current_wal_flush_lsn() AS flushed;

The flush LSN is past the COMMIT record: the commit rule held before COMMIT returned. HOT_UPDATE is the heap-only update from Pages, tuples and heap files, which writes the new row version on the same page and leaves the index alone. VACUUM first cleared out the old versions the first refund left, so the dump shows only this refund. Your LSNs will differ.

sections.h: After a crash: replay the log from the last checkpoint
sections.html:
After a crash, the table's files are a mix. Some pages have every committed change, some are minutes behind, and the log holds the difference. Recovery reads the log and redoes what the pages are missing. Two questions decide how: where in the log to start, and how to tell whether a page already has a change.

Starting at the beginning of the log would work, but it could take hours, and the log would have to be kept forever. A checkpoint sets a limit. It writes every dirty page to the files, forces them to disk, then logs a checkpoint record that names the redo point, where recovery may start. PostgreSQL keeps the location of the latest checkpoint in a small file, global/pg_control. Every change before the redo point is sure to be in the files, so recovery starts there, and older log files can be reused. PostgreSQL runs a checkpoint every 5 minutes (checkpoint_timeout), or sooner when about 1 GB of log has piled up (max_wal_size). It spreads the page writes over most of that time.

On the whiteboard, a checkpoint is a photo. After a wipe, start from the last photo and replay the notebook lines written after it.

The page LSN answers the second question. Recovery applies a change only if the page's LSN is below the position of the record. If the page reached the disk after that change, its LSN already covers it, and the record is skipped. That makes redo idempotent: doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once. If the power fails again during recovery, the next recovery replays the same records and ends in the same state. The stepper runs a whole recovery.

What about transactions that never committed? Their records can be in the log on disk, flushed by someone else's commit, like T2 in the stepper. Here the whiteboard picture breaks: every notebook line counts, but a database log also holds records of transactions that never finished, and recovery must leave them out. In an engine that writes unfinished changes into its pages, they can be on disk too. The lab never lets unfinished changes into pages, so its recovery drops their records.

Real engines follow ARIES, the recovery design that IBM published in 1992. In plain words, it makes three passes over the log:

  1. Analysis reads from the last checkpoint to the end of the log. It works out which transactions were still open at the crash (the losers) and which pages may be missing changes.
  2. Redo replays every change from the redo point, committed or not, wherever a page's LSN shows it's missing. ARIES calls this repeating history: afterwards, the pages look exactly as they did at the moment of the crash.
  3. Undo rolls the losers back, newest change first, using undo information they logged. It logs each undo step too, so a crash during recovery never undoes the same change twice.

InnoDB, the part of MySQL that stores data, and Oracle follow this design. PostgreSQL repeats history like ARIES but has no undo pass at all. A transaction with no commit record counts as aborted, cancelled. Every row version it wrote is stamped with its id in t_xmin, as Pages, tuples and heap files showed, and is invisible to every query. The Transactions track's lesson on MVCC, PostgreSQL's way of keeping several versions of each row, covers those rules. In the Try it, the loser's row version is still on the page after recovery, and nobody can see it.

The log ends where its records stop checking out: at the first record that is short or fails its CRC. That's the checksum from Bytes, pages and durability: a number worked out from the record's bytes, which changes if any byte does. PostgreSQL logs that point as invalid record length. Next, we'll meet the one crash this replay can't fix alone.

try.title: Pull the plug with a transaction open
steps: In a first terminal window, open psql, start a transaction that sets account 3 to zero, and leave it open: don't type COMMIT.

In a second terminal, in the labs folder, commit an update to account 4 and note the checkpoint's redo_lsn, its redo point. Then kill the server the way a power cut would (SIGKILL gives it no chance to tidy up) and start it again. Predict where redo starts.

Before anything else reads the table, look at page 0 with pageinspect, an add-on that shows the raw contents of pages. Ask for the status of the transaction that was left open, then read both accounts. Predict what each shows.

sections.h: The one crash the log can't fix alone: a torn page
sections.html:
There's one crash that redo can't fix on its own. PostgreSQL writes 8 KB pages, but a drive only promises to write whole sectors, its own smaller units of 512 bytes or 4 KB. If the power fails in the middle of a page write, the page on disk can be half new and half old: a torn page. A log record like "set the balance in row 14" assumes an intact page, and replayed onto a torn one, it makes garbage. Data checksums, a number stored with each page that changes if any byte does, are on by default for new databases since PostgreSQL 18. They detect a torn page, but they can't repair it.

InnoDB's answer is the doublewrite buffer. It writes each batch of dirty pages first to a separate doublewrite area, forces it, and only then writes the pages in place. After a crash, a torn page has a whole copy to restore from. The first write is one big sequential chunk with a single fsync, so it costs far less than writing everything twice. Facebook's MyRocks paper still names it as one reason InnoDB wrote so much to flash storage, in the numbers that LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters compared.

PostgreSQL does it inside the log, with full-page writes. The first time a page changes after a checkpoint, its log record carries an image of the whole page, a full-page image (FPI). Recovery starts at a checkpoint, so the first record it finds for any page is that image. It restores the page from the image, torn or not, and replays the later small records on top. Further changes to the page before the next checkpoint log only the change.

You pay in log volume right after each checkpoint. In the Try it, 200 updates spread over 120 pages write 902 KB of log just after a checkpoint. The same updates, run again a moment later, write 21 KB: 120 page images, then none. That's the real trade-off in spacing checkpoints. Frequent checkpoints mean a short recovery and more page images; rare ones mean less log and a longer recovery. wal_compression shrinks the images, with LZ4 and Zstandard available since PostgreSQL 15: the same burst wrote 303 KB with lz4.

Leave full_page_writes on. The docs allow turning it off only on a file system that prevents partial page writes itself, such as ZFS. And this is why the append-only store in Bytes, pages and durability never needed any of it: it never overwrites a page that holds live data.

So the log makes every commit cheap and safe. It charges in two places: extra log right after each checkpoint, and a recovery that grows with the time between checkpoints. What it can't do is make a read fast. Finding rows quickly is still the job of the indexes from B+trees.

try.title: Count full-page images
steps: Create wallets, fill it with 20,000 rows, and read it once with count(*). Note how many pages it has.
Run a CHECKPOINT, then the same 200 updates twice, and compare fpi and bytes on the WAL line. Predict the number of full-page images in the first run.
Turn on lz4 compression for your session, checkpoint again, and repeat. When you're done with this lesson, stop PostgreSQL and delete its data: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

opening:
Picture a café owner pressing Refund on her screen. The payments app takes 25.00 from her shop's balance, adds it to a customer's, and the screen says Refunded. A second later, the power fails where the app's database runs. When it comes back, both balances must have changed, or neither. Half a refund is money that vanished.

When the screen said Refunded, neither balance had changed on disk. The database had added about 200 bytes to the end of one file, nothing more.

It's natural to think "saved" means the table on disk holds the new numbers. Saving a document works that way: press save, and the file changes. A database is more careful, and also faster.

In LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters, a log sat beside the memtable, unopened. In this lesson, we'll open it: what a commit writes, the two rules that make the log safe, how a database rebuilds itself after a crash, and the one crash a log of small notes can't fix alone. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a refund that the screen called done while neither balance on disk had changed. It was safe all along: 200 bytes of log, forced at COMMIT, held everything needed to rebuild both pages, and the page LSNs told recovery what was already there.

On any PostgreSQL database you can reach, run SHOW synchronous_commit;, SHOW fsync; and SHOW full_page_writes;. All three should say on. If one doesn't, find out who turned it off, and why.

Next, we'll go back to the B+tree and learn to read EXPLAIN, PostgreSQL's account of how it ran a query. Why does a query with an index sometimes read the whole table anyway?

compare.title: After a crash, a transaction that never committed: the lab and PostgreSQL

a.label: Your lab
a.title: changes reach the pages at commit
a.html:
while running:  UPDATE records are logged,
                pages are NOT changed

recovery:       collect UPDATEs per transaction
                at its COMMIT: apply them where
                  page LSN < commit end LSN
                no COMMIT: drop its records

undo needed:    never: no page held the change

b.label: PostgreSQL
b.title: changes reach the pages at once
b.html:
while running:  each change is logged AND
                written into the page (in memory),
                the page may reach disk (steal)

recovery:       redo every record where
                  page LSN < record end LSN,
                  committed or not
                no COMMIT: transaction counts as aborted

undo needed:    none: MVCC hides the aborted
                row versions; VACUUM removes them

compare.note: Both need only redo, for different reasons. The lab never lets an unfinished change into a page. That's simple, but a long transaction would have to hold all its changes in memory. PostgreSQL lets changes into pages at once and relies on visibility. Every row version carries the id of the transaction that wrote it, and a transaction with no commit record counts as aborted, so MVCC, PostgreSQL's way of keeping several versions of a row, hides it, and VACUUM, its clean-up job, removes it later. Engines that follow ARIES, such as InnoDB and Oracle, take a third way: redo everything, then run an undo pass with undo records.

worked.title: Choose the redo point when a transaction is open during a checkpoint

steps.say: Here is the lab's log after a crash, with records of 29 bytes. T1 committed long ago. T2 began at LSN 116 and was still open when the checkpoint ran. T3 ran after the checkpoint, and T2 committed last.
steps.code:
116 BEGIN  T2
145 UPD    T2  page 3 = 50
174 CHECKPOINT  redo LSN = 116
203 BEGIN  T3
232 UPD    T3  page 1 = 600
261 COMMIT T3  (ends at 290)
290 COMMIT T2  (ends at 319)

steps.say: Find the start. The control file points at the checkpoint record at 174, and its redo LSN is 116, not 174: the checkpoint chose the BEGIN of the oldest open transaction. The pages the checkpoint wrote are on disk with their LSNs.
steps.code:
on disk: page 1 = 700, LSN 116   (flushed by the checkpoint)
         page 3 = 0,   LSN 0

steps.say: Replay from 116. At T3's COMMIT (ending at 290), page 1's LSN of 116 is below 290, so apply 600. At T2's COMMIT (ending at 319), page 3's LSN of 0 is below 319, so apply 50.
steps.code: val pending = HashMap<Int, LinkedHashMap<Int, Long>>() for (r in wal.recover(start = 116)) when (r.type) { UPDATE -> pending.getOrPut(r.txId) { LinkedHashMap() }[r.pageId] = r.value COMMIT -> for ((id, v) in pending.remove(r.txId).orEmpty()) { val p = page(id) if (p.lsn < r.endLsn) { p.value = v; p.lsn = r.endLsn } // T3: page 1, T2: page 3 } else -> {} }

steps.say: Check the alternative. Had the checkpoint used its own LSN, 174, as the redo point, recovery would start after T2's UPDATE at 145. It would see T2's COMMIT with nothing to apply, and lose page 3 = 50. A transaction open across a checkpoint is why the redo point can be older than the checkpoint record. PostgreSQL's redo point is earlier than its checkpoint record for a related reason: changes keep arriving while a checkpoint writes pages.
steps.code: redo LSN = BEGIN of the oldest open transaction, or the checkpoint's own LSN if none is open

In checkpoint, the redo LSN is active.values.minOfOrNull { it.firstLsn } ?: wal.nextLsn. Flush the CHECKPOINT record before control.write, or a crash could leave the control file pointing at a record that isn't on disk.

drill.title: Write recovery from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write recover() for a store whose log has BEGIN, UPDATE (page, value), COMMIT, ABORT and CHECKPOINT (value = redo LSN) records, whose control file holds the LSN of the last checkpoint record, and whose pages carry an lsn. Changes reach pages only at commit. Then answer: what makes running it twice safe?

answer.html: private fun recover() { val checkpoint = control.read()?.let { wal.readAt(it) } val start = checkpoint?.value ?: 0L // redo LSN, or the start of the log val records = wal.recover(start) // stops at the torn tail and truncates it val pending = HashMap<Int, LinkedHashMap<Int, Long>>() var redone = 0 for (r in records) { when (r.type) { RecordType.BEGIN -> pending[r.txId] = LinkedHashMap() RecordType.UPDATE -> pending.getOrPut(r.txId) { LinkedHashMap() }[r.pageId] = r.value RecordType.COMMIT -> for ((id, v) in pending.remove(r.txId).orEmpty()) { val p = page(id) if (p.lsn < r.endLsn) { // the page doesn't have this commit yet p.value = v; p.lsn = r.endLsn; p.dirty = true; redone++ } } RecordType.ABORT -> pending.remove(r.txId) RecordType.CHECKPOINT -> {} } } lastRecovery = RecoveryStats(records.size, redone) // what is left in pending never committed } // The page LSN check: a change is applied only to a page whose LSN is older than the commit, // and applying it sets the LSN, so a second run skips everything the first one did.

recap: A commit adds records to the write-ahead log and forces it to disk. The changed pages stay dirty in memory and are written later.
The commit rule: COMMIT returns only once the log is on disk past the commit record. The WAL rule: a page is written only once the log is on disk up to the page's LSN.
Every page carries the LSN of the last record that changed it. Recovery applies a record only to a page with an older LSN, so running redo twice is safe.
A checkpoint writes the dirty pages and records a redo point, which pg_control points to. Recovery starts there and ends at the first invalid record.
After a checkpoint, the first change to each page logs a whole copy of the page, so a torn page can be restored. The log grows fastest right after each checkpoint.
The limit: the promises hold only while the settings do. synchronous_commit = off can lose the last few transactions but never half of one, while fsync = off can corrupt the database.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "A database must write our balances into the table's file before COMMIT returns, or a crash would lose them." Explain what really happens at COMMIT, and how the balances come back after a crash.
explain.answer: At COMMIT, PostgreSQL forces the write-ahead log to disk, not the table's file. Every change was already described by a small log record, and the commit record goes last. Once the log is on disk past it, COMMIT returns. The changed pages stay in memory and are written later, by a background process or a checkpoint, and never before the log covers them. If the server crashes first, recovery starts at the redo point of the last checkpoint and replays the log onto the pages. It skips any change a page already has, which it can tell from the LSN stamped in each page. So the balances come back from the log. This is also faster than writing pages at commit, because the log is one stream written in order and shared by many commits, while the table's pages are scattered over the file.

deeper.html:
Steal and no-force. Recovery papers name the two freedoms this lesson describes. No-force: a commit doesn't write its pages. Steal: a dirty page may be written before its transaction commits, when the buffer pool needs the room. PostgreSQL, InnoDB and Oracle allow both, which is why their logs must support redo, and, without PostgreSQL's row versions, undo too. The lab is no-steal, which is why it needs redo only.

Checkpoints that don't stop the world. A checkpoint that froze every change while it wrote gigabytes of dirty pages would stall the database for seconds. PostgreSQL notes the redo point when a checkpoint starts, then spreads the page writes over 90% of the time until the next one (checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9) while new changes keep arriving. ARIES calls this a fuzzy checkpoint. The pages on disk never form one consistent snapshot, and they don't need to, because recovery replays from the redo point anyway and the page LSNs sort out the rest.

SQLite's two modes. By default, SQLite copies original pages to a rollback journal, writes the database file, and commits by deleting the journal. In WAL mode, available since SQLite 3.7.0, a commit appends a commit record to a -wal file and doesn't touch the database file. A checkpoint copies pages back, automatically once the WAL reaches 1,000 pages.

Commits in the same breath. One fsync makes every byte before it durable, so PostgreSQL commits that arrive together share one flush. commit_delay (0 by default) makes a committing session wait a few microseconds for others to join, when at least commit_siblings (5) other transactions are active. On fast modern SSDs it rarely helps.

Other databases, same idea. Oracle's log writer process (LGWR) writes the redo log at COMMIT, and its database writer (DBWR) writes data blocks later; it keeps undo in undo segments to roll back unfinished work, as ARIES does. A Cassandra node's default commitlog_sync is periodic, every 10 seconds, so a single node says a write is done before its log is forced, and relies on copies on other computers to keep it.

Replicas are replay that never ends. A PostgreSQL streaming replica, a copy of the database on another computer that follows the main one, receives the main server's log and runs the same redo code that crash recovery uses, forever. That's why a replica's pages are byte-for-byte the same as the main server's, and why the Replication track can treat replication as shipping a log.
